titleText.es: Esto es una historia verdaderamente real, pero ella no sabe que la he puesto en un cómic porque su wifi no funciona desde hace semanas.
titleText.en: This really is a true story, and she doesn't know I put it in my comic because her wifi hasn't worked for weeks.
titleText.noteEn: The narrator says the events really happened and jokes that the woman has not discovered the comic because her wireless connection has been down for weeks.

applications.explanationEn: Historia names the thing first, and the neutral descriptive adjective real follows it.
Real has one singular form for both genders, so it already matches the feminine singular noun historia.

excludedUnits.rationale: This numeral labels the first week in the sequence; it is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: HOLA, SOY LA PRIMA. TENGO UN ORDENADOR NUEVO PERO NO QUIERO WINDOWS. ¿PUEDES AYUDARME A INSTALAR "LINUX"?

excludedUnits.rationale: Windows is the unchanged English-language product name of the operating system, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Ordenador names the thing first, and the neutral descriptive adjective nuevo follows it.
Nuevo uses masculine singular -o to match the masculine singular noun ordenador.
Puedes changes for one familiar listener, while ayudar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside ayudarme.
Ayudarme identifies the speaker as the person receiving help, a is the required link, and instalar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Me attaches directly to the unchanged verb ayudar and identifies the speaker as the person receiving help.

excludedUnits.rationale: This numeral labels the second week in the sequence; it is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: DICE QUE MI XORG ESTÁ ROTO. ¿QUÉ ES UN "XORG"? ¿DÓNDE PUEDO BUSCARLO?

excludedUnits.rationale: Xorg is the unchanged proper name of display-server software, not a Spanish lexical word.
This repeated Xorg label is the unchanged proper name of software, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Está presents the current condition, and roto is the masculine singular describing form used for the software system.
Roto is romper's irregular completed-action form; the regular-looking form rompido is not used.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks what something is.
Dónde carries a written accent because it directly asks for a place or source.
Puedo changes for the speaker, while buscar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside buscarlo.
Lo attaches directly to buscar and stands for the masculine technical item being looked up.

regions.labelEs: MMM, DEJA QUE TE ENSEÑE LAS PÁGINAS MAN.

excludedUnits.rationale: man is the Unix command and borrowed technical label for a manual page, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Deja is dejar's positive command form for one familiar listener.

applications.exampleEs: DEJA QUE TE ENSEÑE LAS PÁGINAS
applications.explanationEn: Deja asks for permission, que introduces the allowed action, te identifies its recipient, enseñe is the special allowed-action form, and las páginas fill the object slot.

excludedUnits.rationale: This numeral labels the sixth week in the sequence; it is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: POR PROBLEMAS CON AUTOCONFIG, ME VOY A PASAR DE UBUNTU A DEBIAN.

excludedUnits.rationale: AUTOCONFIG is unchanged English computing shorthand for automatic configuration, not a Spanish lexical word.
Ubuntu is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
Debian is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Voy changes for the speaker, a links it to the planned action, and pasar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Pasar gives the change, de marks Ubuntu as the starting system, and a marks Debian as the endpoint.

excludedUnits.rationale: Gentoo is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
This numeral labels the twelfth week in the sequence; it is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: HACE SEMANAS QUE NO COGES EL TELÉFONO.

applications.exampleEs: HACE SEMANAS QUE NO COGES EL TELÉFONO
applications.explanationEn: Hace semanas measures the elapsed period, que connects it to a situation continuing through now, and the remaining words supply that negative situation.
Coges changes for one familiar listener, and el teléfono names the call device being picked up or answered.

regions.labelEs: NO PUEDO DORMIR. DEBO COMPILAR EL KERNEL.

excludedUnits.rationale: kernel is the unchanged English computing term for the operating system's core, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Puedo changes for the speaker, while dormir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Debo carries the speaker's obligation, while compilar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: PADRES: HABLAD CON VUESTROS HIJOS SOBRE LINUX. ANTES DE QUE LO HAGA OTRO.

applications.explanationEn: Hablad replaces hablar's final -r with -d to form a positive command for vosotros or vosotras.
The -d command ending in hablad and the possessive vuestros both address several people informally in the forms used mainly in Spain.

applications.exampleEs: ANTES DE QUE LO HAGA OTRO
applications.explanationEn: Antes de que introduces a still-pending event, lo is its object, haga is the special pending-event form of hacer, and otro supplies the subject.

cards.promptEs: de instalar Linux a compilar el kernel
cards.answerEn: The comic compresses a Linux learner's rapid progress from a basic installation request to reading Unix manuals, switching distributions, and building a custom kernel.
cards.noteEn: Xorg is a display system; Ubuntu, Debian, and Gentoo are Linux distributions; and the kernel is the operating system's core. Moving through those topics in a few weeks signals increasingly advanced and obsessive involvement. The final warning copies the tone of a parental public-service announcement for the joke.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Ayudarme combines ayudar, “to help,” with me, which identifies the speaker as the person receiving help. The short word attaches to the unchanged verb ending in -ar.

cards.promptEs: ayudar a alguien a + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone helps another person do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ayudar with the person receiving help, then a and the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The person can be a short word such as me, te, or le: me ayuda, te ayudamos, or ayudarle. The a before the following action is required. That action stays in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir; only the first verb changes when needed.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Dice is a present form of decir used with one person or thing. A report, text, or analysis can be the thing that “says” or indicates information.

example.es: El informe dice que todo está bien.
example.en: The report says that everything is fine.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.promptEs: estar + palabra que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe how someone or something is feeling or doing at a particular time?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by a describing word for the state.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to match who or what has the state: estoy means “I am,” está means “he, she, or it is,” and están means “they are.” The describing word matches the person or thing in gender and number: enfadado, enfadada, enfadados, or enfadadas. This pattern presents the quality as a condition or state; ser is normally used for identity or a defining description.

Roto is the form used after haber in phrases such as he roto (“I have broken”). This kind of form is called a past participle. It can also describe a noun; then its ending matches that noun: un vaso roto but una ventana rota.
cards.questionEn: What special form of romper (“to break”) means “broken”?

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Dónde carries a written accent when it directly or indirectly asks about a location. In a direct question, Spanish also uses the opening question mark ¿.

cards.answerEn: to look it up; to search for it
cards.noteEn: Buscarlo combines buscar, “to look for or look up,” with lo, “it.” Lo attaches to the unchanged verb and points back to a masculine thing already mentioned.

example.es: Voy a buscarlo en el manual.
example.en: I am going to look it up in the manual.

cards.answerEn: hmm; a sound of hesitation or thought
cards.noteEn: Mmm represents a pause while someone thinks, hesitates, or considers an idea.
Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally. Before que and another action, it asks that person to allow the action.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: dejar que otra persona haga algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets or allows another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then que, then put the allowed action in its special requested-action form; state the person when the context does not already make them clear.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive because the action is being allowed or requested, not stated as an established fact. For example, ordinary decide changes to decida, and ordinary busco changes to busque. The person can be explicit, as in deja que Ana decida, or understood from the action form and situation, as in deja que busque, “let me search.” Dejar changes for the person and time; que remains unchanged.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the allowed action
cards.noteEn: After a form of dejar meaning “let” or “allow,” que introduces the allowed action. The person doing that action may be stated after que or understood from the situation and the verb form.
Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

cards.answerEn: I show; I teach (special form after deja que)
cards.noteEn: The ordinary speaker form is enseño. After deja que asks to allow the action, enseño changes to enseñe, a form used for an allowed or requested action rather than a stated fact.

example.es: Deja que te enseñe el mapa.
example.en: Let me show you the map.

cards.noteEn: In a computing context, páginas can refer to pages of technical documentation. A página man is a Unix-style reference page opened with the man command.

cards.answerEn: Unix-like systems provide reference manuals called man pages; RTFM is a rude instruction to read the manual before asking for help
cards.noteEn: The command man opens documentation for commands, programs, file formats, and system calls. RTFM expands to “read the fucking manual.” It is longstanding computing jargon and can sound hostile or dismissive, even when used jokingly.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
to switch; to move (from one thing to another)
cards.noteEn: Pasar has several meanings. With de for a starting point and a for an endpoint, it describes changing from one option, stage, or system to another.

example.en: We switched from the train to the bus.

cards.promptEs: pasar de + punto inicial + a + punto final
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something switches from one option or stage to another?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of pasar, then de before the starting point and a before the endpoint.
cards.noteEn: Pasar changes for the person and time. De and a mark the two ends of the change and both remain visible, even when the endpoints are names, systems, or ideas rather than places.

example.es: Pasamos de una idea a un plan.
example.en: We moved from an idea to a plan.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces the endpoint of a change
it has been; for (introducing elapsed time)
cards.noteEn: Before an amount of time and que, hace measures how long a situation has continued. It is an impersonal form of hacer: it stays hace rather than changing to match a person.

example.es: Hace una semana que estudio aquí.
example.en: I have studied here for a week.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a situation started an amount of time ago and is still continuing?
cards.answerEn: Use hace, then the amount of time, then que and the continuing situation.
cards.noteEn: Hace stays unchanged and measures the elapsed period. Que connects that period to a situation that continues through now. This differs from hace + time used with a finished event: Llegó hace dos días means ‘She arrived two days ago,’ while Hace dos días que está aquí means ‘She has been here for two days.’

example.es: Hace dos meses que trabajo aquí.
example.en: I have worked here for two months.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; connects an elapsed period to a situation still continuing
cards.noteEn: In hace + amount of time + que + situation, que connects the measured time to what has continued through the present. Natural English usually expresses the connection with ‘for.’

example.en: It has been raining for three days.

cards.answerEn: you pick up; you answer (the phone, informal singular)
cards.noteEn: Coges is the present form of coger for one familiar listener. With el teléfono, it commonly means picking up or answering the phone in Spain.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone picks up or answers the phone?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of coger followed by el teléfono.
cards.noteEn: Coger changes for the person and time: cojo, coges, cogió. This telephone expression is common in Spain. In regions where coger can sound vulgar, contestar el teléfono or atender el teléfono is a safer alternative.
Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.
Debo is the present form of deber used by the speaker. A following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

cards.answerEn: to compile (convert source code into an executable form)
talk; speak (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Hablad is the positive command for vosotros or vosotras, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. It comes from hablar by replacing the final -r with -d.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para vosotros: hablad, comed, escribid
cards.questionEn: How do you tell several people informally to do something in Spain?
cards.answerEn: For most verbs, remove the final -r from the verb's dictionary form and add -d: hablar becomes hablad.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This positive command is used with vosotros or vosotras, mainly in Spain. If a short object word such as me is included, attach it to the end: ayudad + me becomes ayudadme.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before masculine plural things)

cards.noteEn: Hijos can mean sons, but the masculine plural also commonly refers to a group of children that includes a daughter.

example.es: Tienen un hijo y una hija: dos hijos en total.
example.en: They have a son and a daughter: two children in total.

cards.noteEn: Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

cards.questionEn: How do you connect one event to a later event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de que, then put the pending event's verb in the subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used after this connector because the later event has not happened yet. For regular -ar verbs, this form uses an e ending: lanzar becomes lance. If one person performs both actions, Spanish often uses antes de plus the second verb's unchanged dictionary form instead: como antes de salir means “I eat before leaving.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: De is a required middle piece when antes introduces a full event with que. Translate antes de que as one connector.

example.en: Let's return before it gets dark.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: Que completes the connector before a full event. The following verb uses a special pending-event form called the subjunctive.
Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.
